doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: Guitar influences: Barney Kessel, Charlie Christian and Herb Ellis
summary: Kessel's influence on later guitarists, Christian's influence on Kessel, and a joke about Herb Ellis.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Technically do you think it’s harder to play Charlie Parker type lines on your instrument than let’s say on the saxophone?

I don’t think so. A lot of guitar players I think maybe there’s a lot of them that can play lines like that, bebop lines. But a lot of guitar players, myself included, are really influenced by the straight ahead, mainstream swing guitar, Barney Kessel type things, and all that. As a matter of fact I think Barney Kessel probably influenced more guitar players that are around my age maybe or younger or something, than people give him credit for. Even though he’s not all that older, Barney, of course he’s in bad shape now, I think Barney maybe is like 13 years older than I am, which would make him probably 76 or something like that. He influenced a lot of players.
Yeah. They usually mention Charlie Christian perhaps more than him.
Um hum, Charlie Christian of course.
But he was not around for very long.
That was one of Barney Kessel’s major influences. And the redhead, it was one of his, he talked about him all the time, Herbie Ellis.
Oh. “The redhead?” Is that what you call him?
I call him the redhead, or the farmer — I call him the farmer once in a while because he was born in Farmersville, Texas. He calls me a hillbilly and I call him a farmer.
